label: Feeling unwell
rationale: Saying you feel off, from the general guai ga warui and the work-safe taichou ga warui to being in or out of form.
mixUps: guai ga warui and taichou ga warui both mean 'I don't feel well', and taichou is the safer word at work. choushi ga warui / ii is being off or on form, and also a device acting up. kibun ga warui is feeling sick or faint right now. kimochi warui (in senses) is queasy or gross.

targets.trap: 'I'm sick' as byouki desu sounds like a real illness; for just feeling unwell, the condition is bad, guai ga warui.
partners: kibun (feeling; kibun ga warui = feel sick, also 'be put off')
targets.use: The general 'I'm not feeling well', usually softened to chotto guai warui; others ask guai warui no? or guai dou? (how are you feeling?).
targets.notes: The sets next to it split the job. Taichou ga warui means the same in a more careful word, and it's the safe phrase for calling in sick at work. Choushi ga warui is being off form, and also a machine acting up (pasokon no choushi ga warui). Kibun ga warui is feeling sick or faint right now (in a car, in a crowd). Kimochi warui (in the senses list) is queasy, but also 'gross, creepy'.

example.romaji: chotto guai warui kara, saki ni kaeru ne.
example.ja: ちょっと具合悪いから、先に帰るね。
example.english: I'm not feeling great, so I'll head home early.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto guai ga warui node, kyou wa saki ni kaette mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと具合が悪いので、今日は先に帰ってもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: I'm not feeling well. Would it be all right if I went home early today?

targets.english: not feel well, be under the weather (the safe phrase at work)
targets.use: The stock phrase for calling in sick or cancelling: taichou ga warui node, kyou wa yasumasete kudasai. Casual talk drops ga (chotto taichou warui), and others ask taichou dou? or taichou daijoubu?
targets.notes: A little more neutral than guai ga warui, so it's the safe choice at work; the opposite is taichou ga ii.

example.romaji: gomen, taichou warui kara kyou yasumu.
example.ja: ごめん、体調悪いから今日休む。
example.english: Sorry, I'm not feeling well, so I'm taking today off.

examplePolite.romaji: sumimasen, taichou ga warui node, kyou wa yasumasete kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: すみません、体調が悪いので、今日は休ませてください。
examplePolite.english: I'm sorry, I'm not feeling well. Could I have today off?

targets.trap: A glitchy phone or PC isn't kowareta, which means it has stopped working (sumaho kowareta? is also said as an exaggeration). If it still works, just badly, it's choushi ga warui: sumaho no choushi warui.
partners: guai (condition: guai ga warui = feel unwell)
kaoiro (complexion: kaoiro ga warui = look pale)
me (eyes: me ga warui = poor eyesight)
targets.use: About yourself it's a vague 'I'm off' (kyou chotto choushi warui). Put a body part or a device before no: onaka no choushi ga warui, sumaho no choushi ga warui (my phone's acting up). Ga often drops in casual talk, the opposite is choushi ii, and choushi dou? asks how things are going.
targets.notes: Onaka no choushi ga warui is the discreet way to mention stomach trouble. Choushi ni noru (get carried away) is a separate idiom with the same noun.

example.romaji: saikin, pasokon no choushi warui n da yo ne.
example.ja: 最近、パソコンの調子悪いんだよね。
example.english: My computer's been acting up lately.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou kara chotto onaka no choushi ga warui n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 昨日からちょっとお腹の調子が悪いんです。
examplePolite.english: My stomach's been a bit off since yesterday.

targets.english: be in good shape, going well
partners: guai (condition: guai ga ii = feel well; of a thing, work properly)
kaoiro (complexion: kaoiro ga ii = look well)
kigen (mood: kigen ga ii = be in a good mood)
targets.use: The opposite of choushi ga warui, for your body, your form or a device: kyou choushi ii (I'm on form today), and choushi dou? asks how things are going. Ga often drops.
targets.notes: About someone's words it means glib: choushi ii koto bakari iu (always says whatever suits them).

example.romaji: saikin, karada no choushi ii n da.
example.ja: 最近、体の調子いいんだ。

examplePolite.romaji: saikin, karada no choushi ga ii n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近、体の調子がいいんです。
examplePolite.english: I've been in good shape lately.

targets.english: feel sick (queasy or faint); feel put off
targets.trap: English 'I feel bad (about it)' is guilt, which is warui na or moushiwake nai, never kibun ga warui. Kibun ga warui is feeling sick, or feeling put off by something someone did; a grumpy mood that others can see is kigen ga warui.
partners: kigen (mood: kigen ga warui = be grumpy)
igokochi (comfort: igokochi ga warui = uncomfortable somewhere)
targets.use: For feeling sick right now, in a crowd, a hot room or a car: chotto kibun ga warui (ga can drop, but it's kept far more than in kimochi warui), and kibun waruku natta when it comes on. Said about something someone did, it means it left you feeling put off: ano iikata, kibun warui.
targets.notes: Kimochi warui is the queasier twin with a 'gross' sense; guai ga warui is general unwellness.

example.ja: 電車混んでて、気分悪くなっちゃった。
example.english: The train was packed and I started feeling sick.

examplePolite.romaji: densha ga sugoku konde ite, kibun ga waruku natte shimatta n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 電車がすごく混んでいて、気分が悪くなってしまったんです。
examplePolite.english: The train was really packed, and I started feeling sick.

have good taste, a good eye
go out for fun; go visit
speak to, call out to; ask along
